titleStmt.title: A New Scheduling Algorithm and a Compensation Strategy for Imprecise Computation

analytic.title: A New Scheduling Algorithm and a Compensation Strategy for Imprecise Computation

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: The periodic multiframe task models and the imprecise computation techniques have been developed for scheduling real-time tasks. We introduce the imprecise computation concept into the periodic multiframe task model and derive a novel scheduling algorithm and an error compensation strategy. The paper also pays attention to the imprecise computation input error, which was often neglected in previous studies.

The scheduling algorithm employs an error compensation strategy that based on the traditional Largest-Weight-First algorithm (LWF). The LWF algorithm guarantees that the largest weighted task executes first, thus minimizing the weighted total error in the task set. Our error compensation strategy enhances the error tolerance during the scheduling and takes maximum advantage of the processor idle time to improve the processor utilization.

The experimental results show that the new task model and the new compensation strategy are practical in improving the schedulability and the processor utilization. The high error tolerance results in high schedulability and 100% processor utilization can be achieved in our algorithm. Moreover, the scheduling algorithm is able to deal with tasks whose laxities are loose or tight. Using both the error tolerance coefficient and the error compensation strategy leads to a good tradeoff between the result qualities (QoS) and the available processor time.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: In real-time systems, timing constraint is usually divided into two types, hard and soft, due to the difference of the functional criticalities. Failures of meeting deadlines may arise in high utilization or system overload [3]. A way to avoid timing faults in soft real-time system is to use the imprecise computation technique [1]. As long as the user considers its result quality acceptable, an imprecise computation can degrade gracefully when resources are insufficient and the demands of workloads are high. For many real-time applications, a timely result of a poorer quality is better than a late result of the precise quality. Examples include the multimedia applications, surveillance and collision avoidance systems [4].

In order to yield a balanced tradeoff between the quality of the execution result and the available time, the imprecise computation proposes to maximize the result quality, in other words, minimize the result error. When the flexible jobs are independent of each other, there is no input error. The uncompleted result will not affect its successor. When the dependent flexible jobs are involved, the input is erroneous [1].

Most of the past studies in imprecise computation scheduling neglect the effect of the input error, i.e. i = Error i ( i ), where the error function is only a monotone nonincreasing function of the actual computation time i [1]. When the workload consists of a finite number of jobs: J 1 ,J 2 ,…,J N , the total error = N i=1 w i i , where w i (0,1) are the weights, which indicate different degrees of the influences of J i to the overall quality of the result. The total error is a criterion to qualify a specific strategy of the imprecise computation scheduling. An optimal schedule is defined as a feasible schedule with minimized total error. Therefore, the weighted total error also must be minimized when tasks have different weights [9].

Nowadays, as more periodic multiframe task models are developed in the real-time area, such as the multiframe (MF) task model [7] and the generalized multiframe (GMF) task model [5][8], the imprecise computation technique has not been investigated in the periodic multiframe task models yet. One goal of this paper is to introduce a new task model by incorporating the imprecise computation concept into the multiframe model.

In our task model (called Weighted Modified GMF model), we assume that the executions of the frames (jobs) are carried out sequentially in a task. In order to handle transient overload and enhance fault tolerance, computation time of the frame can be reduced gracefully to meet the deadline as long as the produced result is tolerable. Moreover, even the frame's imprecise computation exceeds the error tolerance threshold; the processor does not reject the task immediately. Instead, the system keeps on checking if the next frame can compensate for its previous frame's error. Therefore, the other goal of this paper is to design an algorithm to take advantage of the processor idle time

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. A modified GMF model is proposed in section 2. It extends the original GMF model to the imprecise computation field, hence becomes an expedient task model to be scheduled in section 3. Section 3 presents a novel imprecise scheduling algorithm based on the Largest-Weight-First (LWF) algorithm. We discuss the implementation and simulation of this algorithm as well as its performance evaluation in section 4. Finally, the conclusions are provided in section 5.

div.head: Task Model
div.p: Formally, a generalized multiframe (GMF) task T is characterized by the 3-tuple (E,D,P) in [5] [8], where E, D and P are N-ary vectors of execution requirements, relative deadlines, and minimum separations, respectively. The original GMF model is one of the increasingly sophisticated models, which focuses on the hard real-time system. Therefore, it turns out that we can put such a practical model on the soft realtime system and the new model can be applied in the imprecise computation area.

Because the modified GMF (MGMF) model is derived from the GMF model, it inherits all the time parameters (E, D, P) from the original one, where the parameters have the similar definitions as GMF's, except that the execution requirement is desirable (not necessary to be the actual) and the deadline is soft. That is (E 0 , E 1 ,…, E N-1 ) for (desirable) execution requirements, (D 0 ,D 1 ,...,D N-1 ) for relative (soft) deadlines and (P 0 ,P 1 ,...,P N-1 ) for minimum separations. The ith (i 0) frame of task T has an arrival time a i , an absolute (soft) deadline a i +d i , and an actual execution requirement i , where a 0 0, and a i+1 a i +P (i mod N) (1) d i =D i and i E (i mod N) (2) The arrival time of the first frame equals 0 (a 0 =0), the successor's arrival time equals its predecessor's arrival time plus the minimum separation (namely, a i+1 =a i +P (i mod N) ). As long as no other competing task exists, this assumption is always correct. Otherwise, the current frame may postpone its execution until the resource (processor) available. The frame can not be executed before its arrival and has to stop executing when the deadline approaches. We adopt the idea of "firm quality" here. It represents flexible resource demands but strict time constraints; the frames degrade gracefully by reducing their demands and resulting qualities [6]. The frame ends when the deadline expires, even if it has not been completed yet. The partial execution produces the imprecise outcome which may be tolerable.

We make another assumption: E i D i P i for 0 i<N. The computation time will never be larger than the relative deadline; otherwise, the task is designed improperly. The precedence constraint within a task requires that a frame must terminate before the next frame starts, hence we require D i P i . All the frames in the task are carried out sequentially; the input of the successor depends on the output of its direct predecessor. In other words, the execution order of frames in a task can not be switched at runtime. Nevertheless, the relationship among tasks is independent. One task's error does not influence another task's execution. The execution order of the tasks is determined by their priorities. We will discuss it in detail soon.

The goal of introducing the MGMF model is obvious -applying it to the imprecise computation area. Therefore, two additional parameters should be included for imprecise computation usage. One is the "error tolerance coefficient", j , which is a real number within the domain [0,1). j = 0 implies that the task T j should be scheduled precisely since no error can be accepted; j approaches 1 while the domain interval does not close at the right side. Apparently, the quality of the task will be poor if its error tolerance reaches 100%. j is given when the task is released for scheduling and is checked during the scheduling. It indicates the final quality acceptable to the user. Any error caused by the frame larger than the threshold plus the error can not be compensated by the successor, the task is "unschedulable" and rejected. The schedulability test stops, and the whole time complexity of the schedulability test is reduced.

The other parameter is "weight". By assigning the weight to each frame, we can assign different degrees of impact to the overall quality of the result [6]. "Weight" is denoted as "W" in a weighted MGMF task model (WMGMF); it is also an N-ary vector (W 0 , W 1 ,...,W N-1 ). Each WMGMF task can have N frames; each frame has its own weight, which indicates the potential influence of that frame over the task. The larger the weight is, the more significant role the frame is in the task. The task's weight is defined as the sum of its frames' weights. However, the motivation of introducing the "weight" concept into the MGMF model is not intended to allow for the execution the largest weighted frame first in the task. The assumption of our new model emphasizes that all the frames in the task are scheduled sequentially. The frames are dependent, and the order of the frames is fixed in that task. The real objective we aim for here is to obtain the priority order among the tasks. The largest weighted task executes first (Largest-Weight-First algorithm [16]); individual frames within the task are tested one by one.
The value of W i is a real number in the domain (0, 1), which is adequate in most cases.

div.head: Largest-Weight-First Algorithm
div.p: The Largest-Weight-First algorithm (called LWF algorithm) assigns higher priorities to larger weighted tasks when doing the scheduling [9]. It has been proven to be optimal in the sense of minimizing the total error when scheduling the tasks with different weights [1] [2]. The frames in our WMGMF task are dependent and executed sequentially. The task's weight equals the sum of its frames' weights. As we have shown in the previous example, higher priority is assigned to T2 over T1. Although W 11 >W 10 , the second frame of T1 must execute after the first one. .

div.head: Error Handling
div.p: Despite the negligence of the input error in most previous researches, it isn't always the case in a real-time system. The imprecise computation should have the capability to handle the erroneous input in the reality. The error in a result is the distance between the obtained result and the precise result [4]. In our WMGMF task model, frames (jobs) are dependent in a task, therefore, only the first frame doesn't have the input error; all the successors may have the erroneous inputs. div.head: Schedulability Test
div.p: Before testing the schedulability of the WMGMF task set, we need some assumptions:
o Tasks in the task set are independent; frames in the task are dependent and executed sequentially; o The execution of the frame is preemptable;

o The overhead of the operating system, such as context switch, is ignored and included in the computation time. o When the ith frame's imprecise computation o error is larger than its threshold, namely ji >FAE ji , the least compensation time (T ji ) needed to correct the error is proportional to the ji :

T ji =E ji × ji ( 7) where E ji is the desirable computation requirement of the ith frame in the task j and ji is the error produced by the ith frame. In other words, the larger the error is, the longer the processor time will cost the successor to adjust the error.

It has been proven that the schedule produced by any preemptive policy over a periodic task set is cyclic [10]. In this sense, the schedulability test for the WMGMF task set only needs to check the schedulability throughout the first hyperperiod (H p , least common multiple of the task periods). The highest priority task is always precisely schedulable as long as the task design is correct. Therefore, if there are n tasks in the task set, eventually only n-1 tasks need to be tested over the first hyperperiod.

The problem of testing the schedulability of the task lies in testing the individual frames within the task. If all the frames are schedulable, the task is then schedulable. div.head: Scheduling Algorithm
div.p: The scheduling algorithm is an off-line algorithm. A list (OL) is used to store all the time slots which have already been occupied by the frames with higher priorities. Each node in the list contains the information of the frame, including the task name, frame number, period number (the position in the H P ), start time and end time. The node is inserted with the following restrictions: the start time of a node must be less than its end time and the start time of a node must be larger than or equal to the end time of its previous node.

To test the schedulability of the frame F ji , the worst case is to go through the whole list to find the slack after the arrival time (a ji ) and before the absolute deadline (abd ji ) of the frame F ji . Precise schedulability is tested first using the function schedule_test: if the slack E ji , the function returns true; otherwise, the function returns false and the function imprecise_test is activated. In the following pseudo codes, subscript k specifies the kth period over the hyperperiod. N represents the total frame number of the task j. F jik is the data structure including all the information of a WMGMF frame, i.e., j , E ji , D ji , P ji , and W ji . Therefore, three for loops are needed in the function main to test each F jik .

The function get_error calculates the error ( jik ) and stores the Frame Acceptable Error (FAE ji ) as the global variables. jik may equal 0 if F jik is precisely schedulable; FAE ji may also be 0 if j equals 0. The function olist_add inserts the new nodes with the start time a jik and end the time a jik +slack into the list OL.

div.head: Simulation
div.p: Each task in the simulation has randomly generated parameters: j , E ji , D ji , P ji and W ji. The restrictions on the parameters are: 0 i<N; E ji D ji P ji ; 0 j <1;0<W ji <1 and n-1 j=0 N-1 i=0 W ji =1. The processor utilization (U) and the ratio of the imprecise completed frames (RIF) are calculated Table 1 shows the statistics of the first 10,000 simulations. In order to determine the variant tendency of the U and the RIF with different task number and different frame number, a second experiment with fixed pairs of task number and frame number was designed.

Furthermore, in order to obtain the statistics of average Us and average RIFs in the different frame laxity (laxity of F ji = D ji -E ji ) conditions, such as E ji D ji (tight laxity) and E ji << D ji (loose laxity), a third experiment was designed.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: The main endeavor of this paper is to introduce the imprecise computation concept into the periodic multiframe task model and to explore a novel scheduling algorithm for the new model. The input error, which was neglected in most previous researches, is well considered in our error function.

The basic idea of our scheduling algorithm is an error compensation strategy based on the traditional Largest-Weight-First algorithm. The LWF algorithm guarantees that the largest weighted task executes first, thus minimizing the weighted total error in the task set. Our error compensation strategy enhances the error tolerance during the scheduling and takes maximum advantage of the processor idle time to improve the processor utilization. Therefore, the theoretical foundation of the proposed algorithm follows the requirement of finding an "optimal schedule" in the imprecise computation area.

With the tremendous growth of the internet in the past few years, simply increasing bandwidth capacity became insufficient to satisfy all the application requirements [11]. Adding QoS (Quality of Service) is significant because it enables a network element to have some level of assurance that its traffic and service requirements can be satisfied. QoS-enabled (high-prority) applications do not disable the low-priority internet applications; the low-priority applications may have a lesser service, but still function [11]. The proposed algorithm is designed for improving the QoS.

Our experimental results show that the new WMGMF model and the new compensation strategy are practical in improving the schedulability and the processor utilization. The RIF can reach 46% in the simulation, indicating that the high error tolerance will result in a high schedulability. Moreover, in 10,000 simulations, we reach 100% maximum U every time, while the average U can exceed 90% with the relatively large number of tasks (Figure 3). The new scheduling algorithm also exhibits the good performance in the third experiment, where both the small task set with tight laxity and the large task set with loose laxity can be handled. Using both the error tolerance coefficient j and the error compensation strategy in the scheduling algorithm leads to a good tradeoff between the result quality (QoS) and the available processor time.
